title: Back Pain: Physical Exam
text: The physical exam should screen function, look for structural clues, assess neurologic status, and use special tests when they fit the clinical picture.

title: Back Pain: Physical Exam
text:
General functional screen: 3S
Use 3S as a quick screen of function.

Sit-to-stand
Observe whether the patient can rise from a chair comfortably and without assistance.


Stance
Observe whether the patient can fully straighten once standing, maintain balance, and show normal spinal alignment.
Also look for symmetry of the shoulders, hips, and knees.


Stride
Observe gait.
Look for:

Normal gait pattern
Normal stride length
Ability to turn safely and efficiently

title: Back Pain: Physical Exam
text:
Inspection and palpation
Inspection and palpation should be focused on the area of pain, but the exam should also consider nearby joints because hip, knee, or ankle problems can contribute to perceived back pain.

Inspection: SEADS
Look for:

Swelling
Erythema
Atrophy
Deformities
Skin changes



Palpation: TESTCA
Assess for:

Tenderness
Effusion
Swelling
Temperature
Crepitus
Atrophy

title: Back Pain: Physical Exam
text:
Neurologic exam
A neurologic screen is important when radiculopathy or neurologic compromise is possible.
Assess:

Sensation
Power
Reflexes


Sensation: dermatomes
Common lower-limb dermatomes:

L3: medial knee
L4: medial malleolus
L5: dorsum of the foot
S1: lateral foot
S2: posterior thigh



Power: myotomes
Common lower-limb myotomes:

L2: hip flexion
L3: knee extension
L4: ankle dorsiflexion
L5: great toe extension
S1: ankle plantarflexion
S2: knee flexion



Reflexes
Key reflexes:

L3-L4: patellar reflex
S1-S2: Achilles reflex

title: Back Pain: Physical Exam
text:
Spinal deformity tests

Adam’s forward bend test
Ask the patient to stand with their feet together and bend forward at the hips. Assess spinal symmetry from behind.
Asymmetry of the spine or shoulders may suggest scoliosis.


Modified Schober’s test
Mark a horizontal line at the level of the PSIS, then mark 10 cm above and 5 cm below that line. Ask the patient to bend forward and measure the increase in distance.
An increase of less than 5 cm suggests restricted lumbar flexion, which may be seen in inflammatory conditions such as ankylosing spondylitis.

title: Back Pain: Physical Exam
text:
Lumbar radiculopathy tests

Straight leg raise
With the patient supine, raise the symptomatic leg to 30-70 degrees.
A positive test reproduces radiating pain down the leg into the foot. Hamstring tightness alone is not a positive test.


Lasegue sign
After a positive straight leg raise, lower the leg until symptoms improve, then dorsiflex the ankle to re-tension the sciatic nerve.
Reproduction of the same radiating pain supports nerve root irritation.


Crossed straight leg raise
Raise the asymptomatic leg.
Reproduction of pain in the symptomatic leg is more specific for disc herniation.

title: Back Pain: Physical Exam
text:
Sacroiliac joint tests

FABER
Place the leg into a figure-four position while the patient is supine. Apply downward force to the knee while stabilizing the opposite hip.
Pain in the back or buttock supports SI joint involvement. Groin pain suggests hip joint pathology rather than SI joint pathology.


Gaenslen’s test
With the patient supine, hang one leg off the side of the table and bring the other leg toward the chest. Apply gentle downward force to the hanging leg to stress the SI joint.
Pain in the back or buttock supports SI joint involvement.

title: Back Pain: Management
text: Management depends on red flags, symptom severity, functional limitation, psychosocial risk, and response to conservative care.

title: Back Pain: Management
section: First decision: are there red flags?
text:
First decision: are there red flags?
If red flags are present, management should shift toward urgent or emergent referral and appropriate investigations.
If red flags are absent, most patients can start with conservative management.

title: Back Pain: Management
text:
Risk stratification
Patients can be risk-stratified using clinical judgment or an objective tool such as the STarT Back Tool.
A simple approach is to think in terms of low, medium, and high risk.

title: Back Pain: Management
text:
Low-risk patients
Low-risk patients can usually start with self-management.
Core options include:

Education and reassurance
Exercise therapy
Superficial heat therapy
Oral NSAIDs as needed
Follow-up as needed

title: Back Pain: Management
text:
Medium-risk patients
Medium-risk patients may need more support.
Management can include the low-risk strategies plus:

Physiotherapy referral
Consideration of a short-term trial of scheduled oral NSAIDs rather than only as-needed use
Reassessment in 4-6 weeks

title: Back Pain: Management
text:
High-risk patients
High-risk patients often need a more engaged, multidisciplinary approach, especially when pain is chronic, disabling, or strongly influenced by psychological and social factors.
Management may include:

CBT or psychologically informed care to address negative psychological features
Multidisciplinary pain program referral for debilitating chronic low back pain
Closer follow-up and function-focused goal setting

title: Back Pain: Management
section: Adjunctive options with possible benefit in selected cases
text:
Adjunctive options with possible benefit in selected cases
Some treatments may be useful in specific situations.
Examples include:

Duloxetine for chronic low back pain, especially with mood symptoms
Muscle relaxants short-term for acute back pain
Chiropractic manipulation for acute lumbar back pain
Epidural steroid injection for short-term relief of radicular pain
Radiofrequency ablation for refractory facet or SI joint pain

title: Back Pain: Management
text:
Adjunctive options with conflicting evidence
Some treatments have mixed or limited evidence.
Examples include:

Acupuncture, which may have a small effect in chronic nonspecific back pain
Oral cannabinoids, mainly considered in chronic refractory neuropathic pain

title: Back Pain: Management
text:
Options generally not preferred
Some options are ineffective, have insufficient evidence, or have harms that often outweigh benefits.
Examples include:

Acetaminophen
Benzodiazepines
Capsaicin
Gabapentinoids for nonspecific low back pain
Opioids
Oral corticosteroids
TENS/PENS

title: Back Pain: Management
text:
Reassessment
If symptoms meaningfully improve, continue conservative management and follow up as needed.
If symptoms remain function-limiting after conservative care, consider adjunctive interventions, further investigations, or referral depending on the clinical pattern.

title: Back Pain: Introduction
text: Welcome to this module on Back Pain.

title: Back Pain: Introduction
text:
Why this module matters
Back pain is one of the most common complaints you will hear from patients throughout your career. Part of this is because back pain is broad and multifactorial, and is thus encountered in a variety of different specialties, including primary care, hospitalist medicine, emergency medicine, orthopedics, rheumatology, anesthesiology, and physical medicine and rehabilitation.
The purpose of this module is to help you build foundational knowledge and develop a practical framework for approaching back pain in a clinical setting.
At a high level, this framework should help you answer four core clinical questions whenever you see a patient with back pain:






NoteCore clinical questions




Is there anything acutely dangerous that requires urgent intervention?
What specific type of back pain best explains the patient’s symptoms?
How is the pain affecting the patient’s day-to-day functioning and quality of life?

What is the most appropriate next step in management?

title: Back Pain: Introduction
text:
What you will learn
By the end of this module, you should be more comfortable with:

Describing key spine anatomy and common pain generators
Organizing back pain into common clinical patterns
Taking a focused back pain history
Screening for red flags and yellow flags
Performing a practical physical exam
Knowing when investigations are and are not useful
Choosing an initial management plan
Applying the framework to interactive cases

title: Back Pain: Anatomy
text:
Back pain is easier to approach when you think in terms of structures that can generate pain and structures that can be compressed or irritated.
The goal of this section is not to memorize every ligament, muscle, and bony landmark. The goal is to understand the main anatomic structures that help explain common back pain patterns.

title: Back Pain: Anatomy
text:
The lumbar spine
The lumbar spine is made up of five vertebrae, labeled L1 to L5. These vertebrae support much of the body’s weight and allow flexion, extension, rotation, and side-bending.
Each vertebra has a vertebral body in the front and a posterior arch in the back. Together, these structures help form the spinal canal, where the spinal cord and nerve roots travel.
In the lumbar spine, the spinal cord has usually ended by around the L1-L2 level. Below this, the canal contains the cauda equina, a bundle of nerve roots that continues downward before exiting through the foramina.

title: Back Pain: Anatomy
text:
Intervertebral discs
The intervertebral discs sit between vertebral bodies and help absorb load.
Each disc has two major parts:

The annulus fibrosus, which is the tougher outer ring
The nucleus pulposus, which is the softer inner center

Disc-related pain can occur when the disc itself becomes irritated, degenerative, or structurally disrupted. Disc material can also herniate and irritate a nearby nerve root, producing radicular pain.
A simple clinical pattern to remember:






NoteDisc pattern



Disc-related pain is often worse with flexion, bending forward, or prolonged sitting.

title: Back Pain: Anatomy
text:
Facet joints
Facet joints are paired joints at the back of the spine. They help guide and limit spinal movement, especially extension and rotation.
Facet-mediated pain is usually more back-dominant than leg-dominant. It can sometimes refer into the buttock or thigh, but it usually does not follow a clear dermatomal pattern.
A simple clinical pattern to remember:






NoteFacet pattern



Facet-mediated pain is often worse with extension and rotation, and may feel better with flexion.

title: Back Pain: Anatomy
text:
Nerve roots
Lumbar nerve roots exit the spine through openings called neural foramina, which are small side openings formed between neighboring vertebrae.



This image shows a transverse section of the spine. The neural foramen is outlined in green on the right. On the left, the dorsal root and ventral root are shown passing through the neural foramina and joining to form the spinal nerve. Narrowing of the neural foramen can irritate or compress the exiting nerve root and contribute to radicular symptoms.


When a nerve root is compressed or irritated, the patient may develop radiculopathy. This can cause pain, numbness, tingling, weakness, or reflex changes in a nerve-root distribution.
Common lumbar patterns include:

L3: medial knee sensation, knee extension
L4: medial malleolus sensation, ankle dorsiflexion, patellar reflex
L5: dorsum of foot sensation, great toe extension
S1: lateral foot sensation, ankle plantarflexion, Achilles reflex

Radicular pain is usually more leg-dominant and may feel sharp, shooting, burning, or electric.

title: Back Pain: Anatomy
text:
Sacroiliac joint
The sacroiliac joint, or SI joint, connects the sacrum to the ilium of the pelvis. It transfers load between the spine and the lower limbs.
SI joint pain is often felt around the posterior pelvis, buttock, or PSIS region. It can mimic other causes of low back pain, which is why the diagnosis usually depends on the overall clinical pattern rather than a single test.
A simple clinical pattern to remember:






NoteSI joint pattern



SI joint pain is often felt near the posterior pelvis or buttock and may worsen with transitional movements, single-leg loading, or prolonged positions.

title: Back Pain: Anatomy
text:
Spinal canal and foramina
The spinal canal contains the spinal cord in the upper spine and the cauda equina in the lumbar region.
The neural foramina are side openings where nerve roots exit.
Narrowing of these spaces is called stenosis.

Central canal stenosis can compress multiple nerve roots.
Foraminal stenosis can compress a specific exiting nerve root.

Lumbar spinal stenosis often presents with leg symptoms that worsen with standing or walking and improve with sitting or forward flexion.






NoteStenosis pattern



Lumbar spinal stenosis often causes leg heaviness, pain, or fatigue with walking or standing, relieved by sitting or bending forward.

title: Back Pain: Anatomy
text:
Muscles and ligaments
The lumbar spine is supported by muscles, fascia, and ligaments.
Important support structures include:

Paraspinal muscles
Multifidus
Quadratus lumborum
Abdominal wall muscles
Thoracolumbar fascia
Iliolumbar and sacroiliac ligaments

These structures are important because many patients have back pain that is influenced by movement, load, conditioning, posture, and activity tolerance, even when there is no single identifiable structural lesion.

title: Back Pain: Anatomy
text:
Key takeaway
A practical back pain assessment does not require identifying one perfect pain generator in every patient.
Instead, anatomy helps you ask better clinical questions:

Is this back-dominant or leg-dominant?
Is there a neurologic pattern?
Does the pain behave mechanically?
Does the pattern suggest disc, facet, SI joint, stenosis, or nonspecific mechanical pain?
Are there red flags suggesting something more serious?

title: Back Pain: History
text: A focused back pain history should describe the current pain, screen for serious causes, and identify psychosocial or functional factors that may affect recovery.

title: Back Pain: History
text:
Characterize the pain: OPQRST
Use OPQRST to describe the current pain episode.

Onset
Ask when the pain began and whether it started suddenly or gradually.


Palliation and provocation
Ask what helps or worsens the pain.
Useful questions:

Have you tried any medications or treatments that helped?
Are there positions or movements that make the pain better or worse?



Quality
Ask the patient to describe the pain in their own words.
Nociceptive pain is often described as:

Sore
Dull
Aching
Throbbing
Cramping
Tight or stiff

Neuropathic pain is often described as:

Sharp
Stabbing
Shock-like
Burning
Tingling



Region and radiation
Ask the patient to point to where the pain is worst and whether it travels anywhere else.
This helps distinguish back-dominant pain from leg-dominant pain.


Severity
Ask the patient to rate the pain, but remember that the number alone is not enough. Also ask how pain affects function, sleep, work, and activity.


Timing
Ask how the pain has changed over time and whether the patient has had similar pain before.

title: Back Pain: History
text:
Screen for red flags: NIFTI
Use NIFTI to screen for features of serious underlying spinal pathology.

Neurologic
Ask about:

Leg weakness
Sensory deficits
Saddle anesthesia
Bladder or bowel dysfunction



Infection
Ask about:

Fever
IV drug use
Immunosuppression



Fracture
Ask about:

Trauma
Osteoporosis
Fragility risk



Tumor
Ask about:

Prior or current cancer
Unintentional weight loss
Fatigue
Nocturnal pain



Inflammatory
Ask about features suggestive of inflammatory back pain:

Chronic low back pain for more than 3 months
Age of onset under 45 years
Morning stiffness longer than 30 minutes
Improvement with exercise
Disproportionate night pain

title: Back Pain: History
text:
Screen for yellow flags: WORSE
Yellow flags are psychosocial or behavioral features that increase the risk of persistent pain and disability.
Use WORSE as a quick screen.

Worse
Ask whether the patient worries the pain will become worse over time.


Overwhelmed
Ask whether the patient feels overwhelmed or stressed by the pain.


Restrict
Ask whether the patient avoids or restricts activities out of fear of worsening the pain.


Serious
Ask whether the patient believes something serious is causing the pain.


Employment
Ask whether the pain is affecting work, school, or usual responsibilities.

title: Back Pain: History
text:
Function matters
A good back pain history is not only about diagnosis. It should also clarify what the patient is struggling to do.
Ask about:

Walking tolerance
Sitting tolerance
Standing tolerance
Sleep
Work or school demands
Exercise and recreation
Home responsibilities
Goals for return to activity

title: Back Pain: Investigations
text: Most low back pain does not need immediate imaging.

title: Back Pain: Investigations
text:
Key principle
Routine imaging is not recommended for low back pain when there are no red flags.
Initial management is usually conservative, with reassessment after a trial of treatment.

title: Back Pain: Investigations
text:
When to investigate urgently
Urgent referral and possible urgent MRI should be considered when there are red flags, such as:

Major or progressive neurologic deficits
Saddle anesthesia
Bladder or bowel dysfunction
Suspected infection
Suspected malignancy
Suspected fracture
Concerning inflammatory features

title: Back Pain: Investigations
text:
When imaging can be considered
Imaging can be considered when symptoms persist despite an appropriate trial of conservative management, especially if the result would change management.

title: Back Pain: Investigations
text:
Imaging options

X-ray
X-ray can be useful as an initial screen for:

Scoliosis
Spondylolisthesis
Compression fracture, especially with osteoporosis or fragility risk

Limitations:

Poor soft tissue visualization
Often does not change management in uncomplicated low back pain



MRI
MRI provides strong soft tissue visualization and is often the preferred imaging modality when imaging is needed.
MRI is especially useful for:

Radiculopathy
Spinal stenosis
Fracture assessment
Spondylolisthesis assessment
Red flag evaluation

Limitations:

Cost
Wait times
Accessibility
Contraindications such as certain metal foreign bodies or implants



CT
CT is useful for bony anatomy and can be considered when MRI is contraindicated or difficult to access.
Limitations:

Less soft tissue detail than MRI
Radiation exposure

title: Back Pain: Investigations
text:
Non-imaging investigations

EMG/NCS
EMG and nerve conduction studies can be considered when neurologic symptoms are persistent or progressive.
They can help distinguish radiculopathy from other causes of neurologic symptoms, such as peripheral neuropathy.

title: Back Pain: Clinical Patterns
text: Low back pain can be broadly organized into non-specific mechanical pain, specific mechanical pain, and non-mechanical pain.

title: Back Pain: Clinical Patterns
text:
Non-specific mechanical low back pain
This is the most common category. The pain is influenced by movement, loading, or posture, but there is no clear structural pain generator that can be confidently identified.
Typical features may include:

Back-dominant pain
Symptoms that vary with activity, position, or load
No major neurologic deficits
No red flag features

title: Back Pain: Clinical Patterns
text:
Specific mechanical low back pain
Specific mechanical pain follows a more recognizable clinical pattern and may suggest a more specific pain generator.

Discogenic pain
Discogenic pain arises from degeneration or irritation of the intervertebral discs.
Typical pattern:

Back-dominant pain
Worse with flexion or prolonged sitting
Minimal or no neurologic symptoms



Facet-mediated pain
Facet-mediated pain arises from irritation or loading of the facet joints.
Typical pattern:

Localized back pain
Worse with extension or rotation
Often relieved by flexion
May radiate toward the buttocks



Radiculopathy
Radiculopathy occurs when a nerve root is irritated or compressed as it exits the spine.
Typical pattern:

Leg-dominant pain
Shooting, burning, electric, or radiating pain
May follow a dermatomal pattern
May be associated with sensory change, weakness, or reflex changes



Spinal stenosis
Spinal stenosis occurs when narrowing of the spinal canal or foramina compresses neural structures.
Typical pattern:

Bilateral leg pain, heaviness, or fatigue
Worse with walking or standing
Improved with sitting or lumbar flexion
May describe relief when leaning forward, such as on a shopping cart

title: Back Pain: Clinical Patterns
text:
Non-mechanical pain
Non-mechanical pain is less reliably affected by movement or posture and may be more constant. This category includes referred pain from non-spinal structures and serious spinal pathology.
Consider non-mechanical causes when the history includes red flags for infection, fracture, tumor, inflammatory disease, or major neurologic compromise.
